rel.neighbours.text.text: Dominant & subdominant - the keys a fifth away (V and IV). The most basic move; every blues and pop chorus-lift uses them. From C: G and F.

rel.minmed.text.text: A minor third away (C↔E♭ / C↔A). A smooth-but-surprising shift for wonder or scale, no dominant needed. Cinematic - the lift to a final chorus up a minor third.

rel.majmed.text.text: A major third away (C↔E / C↔A♭). The epic chromatic mediant - soaring, otherworldly. Star Wars cues; Coltrane’s Giant Steps cycles through them.

rel.tritone.text.text: A tritone away (C↔F♯). Jazz tritone substitution: swap G7 for D♭7 over a ii-V-I for a chromatic bass. Also the classic menace colour.

rel.dim7.text.text: The symmetric diminished 7th belongs to several keys at once - drop it and modulate almost anywhere. The Romantic-era teleport; silent-film peril stings.

rel.neapolitan.text.text: ♭II, a half-step above the tonic (C→D♭), usually before a cadence. Dark, dramatic weight - Beethoven; the flamenco Spanish sound.

rel.nrlP.text.text: Same root, major ↔ minor (C↔Cm). The most direct mood-flip: a hero’s theme turns minor when they fall. Same melody, opposite feeling.

rel.nrlR.text.text: Relative major/minor, same key signature (C↔Am). The smoothest move - all seven notes shared. Countless verse/chorus pairs.

rel.nrlL.text.text: C↔Em - shares two notes (E and G). A bittersweet, economical voice-leading move; P-L-R chains give smooth chromatic film harmony.

mood.action.traj.note: A mood's .traj is the arc its music takes, shown under the mode in Assist.

mood.running.traj.text: sustained neutral energy, no narrative peak

mood.heroic.traj.text: struggle rising, striving not yet won

lib.axis-progression.name.note: A library name that starts with its numerals keeps them in front with the name in brackets ("I-IV-V (three-chord song)"); the app shows only what is in the brackets.

lib.axis-progression.why.text: Three major chords frame one minor chord, so the loop sounds hopeful with a single shadow, and every rotation can serve as the start.

lib.fifties-progression.why.text: The tonic drops to its relative minor and climbs back through IV and V, the gentle rocking loop of 1950s ballads.

lib.i-iv-vi-v.why.text: The 50s loop with vi and IV swapped, so the minor chord arrives late and V pulls straight back home.

lib.sleep-walk-changes.why.text: The 50s loop with its IV turned minor, which adds a dreamy, bittersweet sigh before the dominant.

lib.three-chord-i-iv-v.why.text: Tonic, subdominant and dominant in their plainest order, the three-chord engine of rock and roll, folk and country.

lib.sonics-i-biii-iv-biii.why.text: Swapping the V of the Louie Louie loop for a borrowed bIII gives the garage-rock riff a darker, bluesier edge.

lib.double-plagal.why.text: bVII falls a fourth to IV and IV a fourth to I, two plagal steps in a row, so the loop feels open and anthemic rather than resolved.

lib.mixolydian-i-bvii-iv-v.why.text: A Mixolydian descent through bVII and IV that turns back up to V, mixing rock swagger with a real cadence.

lib.chromatic-descending-5-6.why.text: Two pairs of chords a fifth apart, the second pair a whole step below the first, so the loop slides down with a relaxed, open sound.

lib.aeolian-shuttle.why.text: The minor tonic steps down two whole steps and back up, a brooding rock loop with no leading tone.

lib.aeolian-descent.why.text: Three chords walk straight down the natural minor scale, a heavy, fatalistic fall that loops back up to the tonic.

lib.creep-progression.why.text: A major III brightens the loop and then IV turns minor, so hope and disappointment trade places every bar.

lib.major-line-cliche.why.text: One inner voice creeps up from the fifth to the sixth and back over a held tonic bass, giving a single chord a sense of motion.

lib.extended-plagal.why.text: Five major chords a fourth apart chain plagal steps all the way home, a long rolling fall into the tonic.

lib.hotel-california.why.text: Each pair of chords falls a fourth, so the minor loop drifts through bright major chords before the dominant pulls it back.

lib.bvii-v7-i-cadence.why.text: A borrowed bVII leans onto the dominant seventh before home, the twangy cadence of 1960s rock and Western scores.

lib.biii-v7-i-cadence.why.text: A borrowed bIII sets up the dominant with a surprising, slightly dark lift before it resolves.

lib.plagal-sigh.why.text: The IV darkens to iv, its sixth sinking a half step onto the fifth of the tonic, a sentimental sigh before home.

lib.i-i7-iv-iv.why.text: The tonic grows a seventh that pulls it to IV, and IV then turns minor, a churchy, bittersweet way back to the start.

lib.puff.why.text: The mediant triad slips in between tonic and subdominant, a soft, folky step that delays the lift to IV.

lib.minor-puff.why.text: The minor tonic rises to its relative major and on to iv, a ballad shape that sounds warm and fatalistic at once.

lib.aeolian-lament.why.text: The Andalusian descent ending on a minor v, so the cadence stays modal and never sharpens to a leading tone.

lib.comfortably-numb-descent.why.text: The lament descent skips the dominant and lands on iv, so the loop sinks without any pull back to the tonic.

lib.pentatonic-minor-ascent.why.text: The roots climb i, bIII, IV, bVI, and the major IV gives a Dorian brightness on the way up.

lib.minor-hopscotch.why.text: The Hopscotch loop heard in minor with a true dominant, so the climb into the tonic gets a sharp leading-tone pull.

lib.major-descending-tetrachord.why.text: The bass walks down 1-7-6-5 under gentle inversions, a major-key cousin of the lament that lands on a half cadence.

lib.magical-mystery-descent.why.text: The bass slides down chromatically under the tonic while IV turns minor, a wistful major-key cousin of the lament.

lib.stairway-descent.why.text: The bass creeps down by half steps under a held minor tonic, turning one chord into a slow, haunted descent.

lib.while-my-guitar-descent.why.text: The bass steps down from the minor tonic through a Dorian IV7 to the flat sixth, a weary, sliding lament.

lib.dream-on-descent.why.text: A half-diminished chord on the raised sixth sits in the middle of the falling bass, borrowing melodic-minor colour on the way down.

lib.ii-v-i-major.why.text: The supertonic and dominant sevenths fall by fifths into a major-seventh tonic, the basic cadence of jazz.

lib.minor-ii-v-i.why.text: A half-diminished ii and an altered dominant fall into a minor tonic, darker and more urgent than the major cadence.

lib.tritone-substitution.why.text: The dominant is swapped for the dominant a tritone away, so the bass slides down by half steps into the tonic.

lib.backdoor-progression.why.text: The tonic is approached from the flat side through borrowed minor chords, a softer, more wistful arrival than V-I.

lib.i-vi-ii-v.why.text: A two-bar circle of fifths that leaves the tonic and arrives back on the dominant, the standard way to keep a tune turning over.

lib.i-vi7-ii7-v7.why.text: Turning vi into a dominant seventh gives the turnaround a secondary-dominant pull into ii, a brighter, more urgent swing.

lib.iii-vi-ii-v.why.text: The circle of fifths started from the mediant, so the turnaround avoids the tonic until the very end.

lib.ragtime-progression.why.text: A chain of dominant sevenths, each resolving down a fifth to the next, bounces back to the tonic.

lib.ragtime-three-chord.why.text: The supertonic becomes a dominant seventh, so it pushes into V like a second leading chord before home.

lib.raised-four-diminished-cadence.why.text: A diminished seventh on the raised fourth leans onto the dominant by half step, a ragtime and parlour cadence.

lib.ii-biii-aug-i.why.text: An augmented chord on bIII shares the dominant's leading tone and adds a raised fifth, a smoky substitute for V.

lib.back-cycled-ii-v-chain.why.text: Each dominant of the ragtime chain gets its own ii, so pairs of chords fall by fifths in a long spiral home.

lib.chromatic-ii-v-chain.why.text: Tritone substitutes put every other chord a half step lower, so the bass walks chromatically down to the tonic.

lib.rhythm-changes-a.why.text: Fast two-beat turnarounds circle the tonic, then a I7-IV-iv move borrows the plagal sigh before the cadence.

lib.rhythm-changes-bridge.why.text: Two bars of each dominant seventh walk the circle of fifths back toward the home key.

lib.montgomery-ward-bridge.why.text: Two ii-V pairs climb a whole step from IV to V, the jazz descendant of the galant Monte sequence.

lib.stomp-progression.why.text: A IV7, raised-fourth diminished and tonic six-four shuffle ends in a ragtime turnaround, the swing-era riff chorus.

lib.coltrane-changes.why.text: Keys a major third apart are each touched by their own dominant, so one cadence spins through three tonal centres.

lib.tune-up-changes.why.text: The same ii-V-I is played and then moved down a whole step, so the key centre sinks like a staircase.

lib.tadd-dameron-turnaround.why.text: Chords borrowed from the flat side fall by fifths and then by half step, a lush chromatic way back to the tonic.

lib.chromatic-turnaround.why.text: Tritone substitutes for vi and V make the bass slide down by half steps from bIII to the tonic.

lib.passing-diminished-turnaround.why.text: A diminished seventh slides down by half step into ii, a gospel-tinged passing chord inside the turnaround.

lib.autumn-leaves-a.why.text: A ii-V-I in the relative major is answered by a ii-V-i in the minor, two cadences linked by the circle of fifths.

lib.all-the-things-a.name.text: Circle of fifths to a new key

lib.all-the-things-a.why.text: Roots fall by fifths from vi to IV, then one dominant lifts the tune a major third into a new key.

lib.lady-bird-changes.why.text: Backdoor ii-Vs visit the flat keys and a closing Dameron turnaround slides home, a sixteen-bar loop full of soft chromatic colour.

lib.solar-changes.why.text: A minor-major tonic opens a chain of ii-V-I cadences that keeps stepping down to new keys until a minor ii-V brings it back.

lib.so-what-form.name.text: Dorian AABA, up a half step

lib.so-what-form.why.text: Sixteen bars on one Dorian minor seventh, eight a half step higher and eight back, so the colour comes from the mode rather than from chord changes.

lib.maiden-voyage-changes.why.text: Suspended dominant chords move in four-bar blocks, so the harmony floats without ever cadencing.

lib.take-the-a-train-a.why.text: Two bars of II7 with a raised fourth in the melody give the tonic a bright, whole-tone lift before a ii-V brings it home.

lib.minor-line-cliche.why.text: One voice slides down by half steps from the root inside a held minor chord, the classic sound of a brooding intro.

lib.twelve-bar-blues.why.text: Four bars of tonic, two of subdominant and a dominant-subdominant turnaround, the call-and-response frame of the blues.

lib.twelve-bar-quick-change.why.text: Bar 2 jumps to IV and back, so the form moves sooner and swings harder than the slow change.

lib.bebop-blues.why.text: The twelve-bar form with ii-V approaches, a raised-fourth diminished and secondary dominants, so every bar points to the next.

lib.bird-blues.why.text: Descending ii-V pairs replace the plain blues chords, spiralling down by whole and half steps before the turnaround.

lib.minor-blues.why.text: The blues form in a minor key, with a bVI7 falling by half step onto the dominant for a darker turnaround.

lib.eight-bar-key-to-the-highway.why.text: The dominant arrives in bar 2, so the short form swings between I, V and IV in quick, conversational phrases.

lib.eight-bar-worried-life.why.text: Two bars each of tonic and subdominant, then a quick I-IV, I-V turnaround, probably the most common eight-bar blues.

lib.eight-bar-heartbreak-hotel.why.text: Four bars of brooding tonic before a short IV-V-I close, a stark eight-bar blues with all its weight up front.

lib.eight-bar-walkin-by-myself.why.text: Four bars on the tonic and then one bar each of IV, V, I and V, an unorthodox eight-bar shape that rushes the ending.

lib.eight-bar-trouble-in-mind.why.text: A minor iv and a secondary dominant give this gospel-tinged eight-bar blues a sweeter, more song-like turn.

lib.eight-bar-sitting-on-top.why.text: The tonic seventh leads to IV and a borrowed iv before a dominant and a double turnaround, a country-blues eight-bar.

lib.eight-bar-aint-nobodys-business.why.text: A major III, a borrowed iv and a vi-ii-V turnaround give the eight bars a torch-song shape.

lib.eight-bar-twelve-minus-four.why.text: Starting on the subdominant drops the listener straight into the second line of a twelve-bar blues.

lib.sixteen-bar-extended-tonic.why.text: Eight bars of stop-time tonic before the usual twelve-bar ending, so the tension builds on one chord.

lib.sixteen-bar-repeated-middle.why.text: The IV-to-I line is sung twice before the turnaround, a folk-blues form that stretches the middle.

lib.sixteen-bar-repeated-turnaround.why.text: The V-IV turnaround is played three times in a row, so the end of the form hangs in a groove before landing.

lib.i-iv-vamp.why.text: Tonic and subdominant rock back and forth, the open, churchy groove behind gospel vamps and soul verses.

lib.gospel-four-five-flat-six-flat-seven.text: Two diatonic steps and two borrowed ones climb by step into the tonic, a dramatic gospel ending.

lib.minor-three-chord.why.text: Minor tonic and subdominant with a major dominant, the harmonic-minor engine of slow jams and street-guitar songs alike.

lib.i-vi-two-chord.why.text: Tonic and relative minor share two notes, so the vamp rocks gently between bright and soft.

lib.pachelbel-canon.why.text: The bass falls a fourth and rises a step in a repeating pattern, so the chords descend gracefully while staying bright.

lib.galant-romanesca.why.text: A stepwise-falling bass under alternating root-position and first-inversion chords, the noble opening gambit of the galant style.

lib.prinner.why.text: The bass steps down 4-3-2-1 under a falling upper line, the galant style's gentle answer to an opening phrase.

lib.fonte.why.text: A cadence onto minor ii is repeated a step lower in the major, so the phrase descends like water from a fountain.

lib.monte.why.text: Each secondary dominant resolves up a step, so the phrase climbs like a mountain path toward the dominant.

lib.ponte.why.text: The dominant is held like a pedal while the melody climbs, a bridge that builds expectation for the return of the tonic.

lib.galant-do-re-mi.why.text: The melody rises do-re-mi over tonic, dominant and tonic again, a simple and confident opening.

lib.meyer.why.text: The tonic moves to the dominant and back while the bass steps 1-2-7-1, a balanced question-and-answer opening.

lib.sol-fa-mi.why.text: The melody falls 5-4-4-3 while the bass rises to ii and returns through the leading tone, a courtly opening gambit.

lib.fenaroli.why.text: Two dominant-tonic pairs with the bass climbing 7-1-2-3, a circular figure that keeps turning around the tonic.

lib.quiescenza.why.text: Over a tonic pedal the upper line sinks to the flat seventh and climbs back, a calm closing gesture after a cadence.

lib.indugio.why.text: The subdominant is lingered on before the bass rises to the raised fourth, a deliberate delay before the cadence.

lib.cadenza-semplice.why.text: The bass climbs 3-4-5 into the dominant and drops to the tonic, the plain galant cadence.

lib.cadenza-composta.why.text: A tonic six-four over the dominant bass delays the V7, the grand compound cadence of classical music.

lib.cadenza-doppia.why.text: The dominant is held while a six-four and a suspended fourth resolve above it, an ornate, ceremonious cadence.

lib.converging-cadence.why.text: The bass climbs chromatically 3-4-#4-5 to a half cadence while the melody falls, the voices converging on the dominant.

lib.galant-deceptive-cadence.why.text: The bass climbs to the dominant and then steps up to vi instead of falling to I, a cadence that sidesteps its goal.

lib.circle-of-fifths-major.why.text: Every diatonic chord is visited by falling fifths, a sequence that feels unstoppable and returns to its start.

lib.circle-of-fifths-minor.why.text: The minor-key circle passes through the relative major before the dominant pulls it back to the minor tonic.

lib.rule-of-the-octave-ascending.why.text: Each step of a rising major-scale bass gets its standard Baroque chord, so a plain scale becomes a full progression.

lib.rule-of-the-octave-descending.why.text: The falling scale is harmonised with a brief tonicisation of V on the sixth degree, a model for accompanying any descending bass.

lib.lament-bass-diatonic.why.text: The bass descends four steps from tonic to dominant under soft minor inversions, the Baroque emblem of grief.

lib.lament-bass-chromatic.why.text: The bass sinks by half steps from tonic to dominant, each chromatic step adding weight to the mourning.

lib.phrygian-half-cadence.why.text: The bass falls a half step from the flat sixth to the dominant, an archaic, questioning close in minor.

lib.ascending-5-6-sequence.why.text: Each chord shares its bass with the next and then the bass steps up, so the music climbs one scale degree at a time.

lib.descending-5-6-sequence.why.text: Root-position chords alternate with first inversions over a stepwise-falling bass, a smooth, singing descent.

lib.rosalia-sequence.why.text: Roots rise a fourth and fall a third, so each pair of chords sits a step above the last in a cheerful climb.

lib.la-folia.why.text: A slow sarabande ground that swings between minor tonic, dominant and the relative major, built for endless variation.

lib.romanesca-ground.why.text: A ground that starts in the relative major and slides into the minor and back, a staple of sixteenth-century improvisation.

lib.passamezzo-antico.why.text: Minor tonic and subtonic alternate, then the relative major and the dominant, the Renaissance ground behind countless dances.

lib.passamezzo-moderno.why.text: Tonic alternates with subdominant and dominant in two balanced strains, the major-key Renaissance ground that folk song inherited.

lib.neapolitan-cadence.why.text: The flat second, voiced over the fourth degree, darkens the approach to the dominant with a poignant half-step fall.

lib.italian-sixth-cadence.why.text: The flat sixth in the bass and a raised fourth above it squeeze outward by half step onto the dominant.

lib.german-sixth-cadence.why.text: A chord that sounds like a dominant seventh on the flat sixth resolves through a cadential six-four, a rich approach to V.

lib.picardy-third.why.text: A minor progression that ends on a major tonic, so the final chord arrives like light after shadow.

lib.tristan-progression.why.text: A half-diminished chord melts onto a dominant seventh that never reaches its tonic, the emblem of Romantic longing.

lib.moravian-cadence.why.text: The outer notes of an added-sixth subdominant move inward by a tone onto a first-inversion tonic, a soft folk-like close.

lib.dorian-shuttle.why.text: The major IV carries the raised sixth of the Dorian mode, so the minor vamp sounds cool and groovy rather than sad.

lib.dorian-i-biii-bvii-iv.why.text: A minor tonic answered at the end by a major IV, so the loop hovers between minor gloom and Dorian brightness.

lib.aeolian-i-bvi-shuttle.why.text: The minor tonic and the major chord on the flat sixth share two notes, a stark, sorrowful two-chord rock.

lib.mixolydian-subtonic-shuttle.why.text: Tonic and the major chord a whole step below alternate with no dominant, the loose, swaggering sound of Mixolydian rock.

lib.lydian-shuttle.why.text: The major II brings in the raised fourth, so the tonic seems to float upward with wonder.

lib.lydian-cadence.why.text: The Lydian II falls to IV and then home, a sunny cadence that avoids the dominant entirely.

lib.phrygian-vamp.why.text: The half step above the minor tonic gives a menacing, exotic pull, the core of Phrygian metal riffs.

lib.phrygian-i-bii-biii.why.text: The riff climbs a half step and then a whole step from the minor tonic, a dark, heaving Phrygian figure.

lib.aeolian-i-bvi-iv-bvii.why.text: The minor tonic falls to bVI and climbs back through iv and bVII, a modal loop with no leading tone.

lib.aeolian-cadence.why.text: Two major chords climb by whole step into a minor tonic, a heroic but sombre arrival.

lib.chromatic-mediant-bvi.why.text: A major chord a major third below shares one note with the tonic, a sudden, glowing shift of colour.

lib.chromatic-mediant-biii.why.text: A major chord a minor third above the tonic shares one note with it, a bold, cinematic lurch.

lib.hexatonic-pole.why.text: A minor chord a major third below the major tonic shares no notes with it, an uncanny, otherworldly shift.

lib.doubly-chromatic-biii.why.text: A minor chord a minor third above the major tonic has no common tones, a dark, disorienting jolt.

lib.imperial-march-mediant.why.text: Two minor chords a major third apart share one note, a progression that film music uses for evil, power and menace.

lib.minor-plagal-shuttle.why.text: A borrowed minor iv over a sustained tonic gives a bittersweet, longing glow.

lib.man-of-steel-progression.why.text: A borrowed bVI between tonic and IV casts a shadow over a heroic major key, heroism with a threat underneath.

lib.interstellar-progression.why.text: A major-seventh bVI and a minor v soften the minor key, so the loop feels vast and less lonely.

lib.mario-cadence.why.text: Two chords borrowed from the minor climb by whole steps into a major tonic, a triumphant fanfare ending.

lib.andalusian-cadence.why.text: Four chords step down the minor tetrachord to a major chord on the fifth, which flamenco hears as a Phrygian home.

lib.andalusian-minor-bvii.why.text: Making the second chord minor smooths the descent and gives the cadence a darker, more modal colour.

lib.solea-por-arriba-letra.why.text: Over two twelve-count compases the tonic rises through its seventh to iv and falls back down the Phrygian tetrachord, the solemn heart of flamenco.

lib.flamenco-cambio.why.text: Moving from bII to bVI briefly sounds like the relative major before the half step back down to the Phrygian tonic.

lib.farruca-compas.why.text: Dominant seventh and minor tonic alternate in four-count bars, a stern, proud minor pulse.

lib.farruca-llamada.why.text: The subdominant leads into a plain minor cadence, the A-minor close that ends farruca phrases.

lib.fandango-de-huelva-copla.why.text: The sung copla leaves the Phrygian tonic for the relative-major area and falls back through bII, the classic fandango shape.

lib.flamenco-guajira.why.text: A Cuban-flavoured major song form in flamenco's twelve-count compas, swinging between tonic and dominant with a vi-ii turn.

lib.girl-from-ipanema-a.why.text: A Lydian-tinged II7 floats over the tonic before a ii and a tritone-substitute dominant glide down by half step home.

lib.blue-bossa-changes.why.text: Minor ii-V-i cadences frame a brief ii-V-I a half step up, a cool, sunlit minor bossa.

lib.i-iv-v-iv.why.text: The V falls back to IV instead of resolving, so the loop circles endlessly, ideal for a dance groove or a montuno.

lib.double-tonic.why.text: The tune swings between a minor tonic and the chord a whole step below, the modal heartbeat of English, Scottish and Irish song.

lib.double-tonic-with-dominant.why.text: The double-tonic shuttle is closed with a real dominant, a tune shape that leads straight into the passamezzo antico.

lib.tonic-dominant-vamp.why.text: Just home and the dominant seventh, the simplest harmonic swing of folk dances, polkas, country and the alegrias compas.

lib.freygish-vamp.why.text: The major tonic of freygish alternates with a minor chord a whole step below, whose third gives a half-step pull back to the tonic.

lib.hijaz-vamp.why.text: The flat second over a major tonic outlines the Hijaz augmented second, a hypnotic, exotic sway.

lib.royal-road.why.text: Subdominant and dominant climb, then the expected tonic is replaced by iii and vi, a bittersweet lift that J-pop choruses love.

lib.royal-road-cadence.why.text: The royal road keeps falling by fifths after vi until it reaches the tonic, turning the loop into a full cadence.

lib.royal-road-secondary-dominants.why.text: Turning iii and vi into dominant sevenths makes the royal road push forward with brighter, more insistent tension.

lib.just-the-two-of-us.why.text: A secondary-dominant III7 tips the key toward its relative minor, then v7-I7 slides back up, a smoky, urban loop.

lib.four-five-six-one.why.text: IV and V rise to vi instead of the tonic, and the tonic follows a bar late, a hopeful loop that keeps stepping upward.

lib.interstate-love-song-descent.why.text: The chromatic lament bass is bent through a half-diminished chord on the raised sixth before landing on the flat sixth.

lib.andalusian-secondary-dominant.why.text: A dominant seventh on bVII tonicises the relative major, so the lament detours through bright chords before the Phrygian close.

lib.fandango-estribillo-circle.why.text: After iv the harmony runs a chain of dominant sevenths down the circle of fifths and drops onto the Phrygian tonic through bII.

lib.farruca-letra-close.why.text: The flat sixth slips down a half step onto the dominant seventh, a stark Spanish minor cadence.

lib.royal-road-minor-form.why.text: The royal-road rise transplanted into minor, climbing from iv and v to the relative major and settling on bVI.

lib.beethoven-lament-german-sixth.why.text: The chromatic bass descends to the flat sixth, where a German sixth and a cadential six-four drive hard onto the dominant.

lib.jupiter.why.text: The melody climbs do-re and leaps up to fa before settling on mi, while the bass steps down to ti and drops to sol, a bright and confident opening.

lib.pastorella.why.text: Over a bass that drops from do to sol and stays there, the melody sways mi-re and then fa-mi, a gentle rustic opening rocking between tonic and dominant.

lib.modulating-prinner.why.text: The Prinner's falling line is moved up a fifth, so the bass walks down do-ti-la-sol and a raised fourth turns the dominant into the new tonic.

lib.passo-indietro.why.text: The bass takes a step back from fa to mi under a dominant seventh, a small backward move that resets the phrase just before a strong cadence.

lib.galant-comma.why.text: The melody falls fa-mi while the bass rises ti-do, the smallest galant close, a light comma at the end of a short phrase rather than a full stop.

lib.galant-evaded-cadence.why.text: A standard cadence approach reaches V, but the bass slips back to mi under a first-inversion tonic, so the phrase dodges its close and keeps going.

lib.chan-chan-son-vamp.why.text: The minor tonic rises to its relative major and the minor subdominant before a major dominant pulls back, an unhurried, wistful son loop for tres and voice.

lib.salsa-minor-montuno.why.text: The minor form of the montuno loop: the major dominant falls back to the minor subdominant instead of resolving, so the piano vamp never quite comes to rest.

lib.how-insensitive-descent.why.text: Over a bass sinking by half steps, the minor tonic passes through a diminished seventh and a minor sixth chord into bright major sevenths, then a minor ii-V closes.

lib.wave-a-section.name.text: Bossa A section with minor iv

lib.wave-a-section.why.text: A flat-six diminished chord slips into v7 and I7 to tonicise IV, which turns minor before a chain of dominants and a minor-plagal turn lead home.

lib.choro-iv-iio-i-cadence.why.text: The minor subdominant passes to the half-diminished supertonic and settles on the minor tonic with no dominant at all, a soft, sighing close that choro uses at section ends.

lib.tsyganochka-circle.why.text: The minor subdominant falls to the tonic and the dominant seventh lands on a major tonic seventh that pulls straight back into iv, so the circle spins and speeds up.

lib.vengerka-dve-gitary-verse.why.text: Each half opens on the minor subdominant, the first dominant slips deceptively up to bVI, and the second resolves home before a major tonic seventh relaunches the verse.

lib.marabi-cycle.why.text: Tonic and subdominant lead to the tonic over its fifth, which leans straight into the dominant, a four-bar cycle built to repeat for as long as people dance.

lib.freygish-i-iv-bvii-cadence.why.text: The major freygish tonic moves to the minor chord on its fourth, then to the minor chord a whole step below the tonic, whose flat second falls by half step back home.

lib.freygish-iv-i-bvii-i.why.text: A long stretch on the minor fourth chord gives way to the major tonic, and the minor chord a whole step below pulls back to it by half step.

lib.mi-sheberakh-bulgar-turn.why.text: The dominant seventh on the second degree carries the raised fourth of the mode, leans on the minor fifth and falls back to the minor tonic before a harmonic-minor V7 closes the phrase.

lib.mogen-ovos-bvii-return.why.text: After a passage in the relative major, a minor chord on the subtonic brings in the flat second, which falls by half step onto the minor tonic.

lib.omnibus-progression.why.text: The bass slides down by half steps while an upper voice climbs against it, so the dominant seventh melts through a second dominant and a minor six-four and comes back, as if the floor moved under a held chord.

lib.common-tone-diminished-seventh.why.text: A diminished seventh slips in over the held tonic note and every other voice moves by half step back into the same chord, a flash of color with no change of function.

lib.ciaccona.why.text: Tonic and dominant frame a dip to the relative minor and a return to the dominant, a short triple-time loop that never closes, so it runs straight into its next repeat.

lib.bergamasca.why.text: Tonic, subdominant, dominant and home in two bars, the plainest full cadence there is, turned into a ground that dancers and players could repeat as long as they liked.

lib.fantasy-fifth.why.text: The raised sixth turns the minor key's fourth chord major, so a dark tonic opens onto a bright chord a fourth up, the sound of a door into another world.

lib.hexatonic-cycle.why.text: Each step changes one note by a half step, alternating major and minor, so six triads circle back to the start without any key taking hold.

lib.shona-mbira-cycle.why.text: Four three-chord phrases each lift one root by a step, so the cycle climbs gently through the scale and drops back to the start, a loop with no strong cadence that can turn for hours.

lib.tritone-sub-two-turnaround.why.text: The secondary dominant II7 is swapped for the dominant a tritone away, so the bass falls by half steps from vi to V and the turnaround slides home chromatically.

lib.ascending-passing-diminished-turnaro.text: A diminished seventh on the raised tonic stands in for VI7 and pushes the bass up a half step into ii, the pull of a secondary dominant with a smoother line.

lib.minor-i-vi-ii-v-turnaround.why.text: The minor-key form of the I-vi-ii-V cycle: half-diminished chords on the raised sixth and on the second step fall by fifths into the dominant, dark but still turning.

lib.gospel-walk-up-to-five.why.text: The bass climbs 3, 4, raised 4, 5 under the chords, so each step tightens the pull and the dominant lands at the top of the climb.

lib.le-sol-fi-sol.why.text: The bass steps down from the flat sixth to the fifth, slips to the raised fourth and climbs back, so the first three chords act like an augmented-sixth approach that wraps the dominant in shadow.
